title: Don't Talk At People
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (andreachiarelli.substack.com), August 9, 2026
summary: Chiarelli examines the common but often invisible habit of 'talking at' people rather than communicating with them, arguing that misunderstanding is a structural feature of language rather than an occasional failure. She explains that shared context, tone, and power dynamics all shape meaning far beyond literal words, and that people routinely overestimate how much common ground they actually share with a listener. She catalogs specific patterns that produce this dynamic -- pre-loaded conclusions, questions with built-in assumptions, topic steering, and premature summarizing -- each of which feels like efficiency or helpfulness from the inside while functionally shutting down genuine exchange. Chiarelli also connects the problem to code-switching, arguing that people who must adapt their language to be heard as credible are doing invisible translation work that listeners often misread as hesitation or weak ideas. She closes with concrete practices -- inviting repair early, offering a 'candidate' rather than a final understanding, delaying solutions, and imagining what's at stake for the other person -- as ways to build conversations where both people end up with a more reliable picture of reality than they started with.
points: Four recognizable patterns of 'talking at' people: pre-loaded conclusions, questions with built-in assumptions, topic steering, and premature summarizing -- all of which feel like efficiency from the inside.
Common ground is routinely overestimated: a colleague's nod usually just means they're tracking the conversation, not that they interpreted your words the way you intended.

Code-switching imposes a hidden cognitive cost: professional register is not neutral, and people doing real-time 'translation work' to be heard as credible are often misread as uncertain or under-prepared.

Practical fix for premature summarizing: 'So what I'm hearing is X, is that right?' positions understanding as provisional and invites correction, unlike 'So what you're saying is X,' which closes the conversation.
Chiarelli's reframe of the goal of conversation: an exchange should end with both people holding a more reliable picture of reality than either had going in.
quotes: Communication is not the transfer of a thought from one head to another, because that is simply impossible. When you say something, you produce a set of words whose meaning is shaped by context, relationship, shared history and more.

The nod you get from your colleague doesn't mean that they have interpreted your words in the same way as you intended. More often than not, it just means they're tracking the conversation, which is quite a different thing.
Pre-loaded conclusions. You open a conversation by presenting the outcome you have already reached, inviting the other person into a conversation that is, functionally, already over.

Code-switching is the adjustment some people make to be taken seriously in that environment. They modify vocabulary, sentence structure, formality, accent and the degree of emotion they allow themselves to show.
Offer a candidate understanding. Paraphrase what you've heard as a test rather than a conclusion.
What we're after is a conversation that ends with both people holding a more reliable picture of reality than either had going in.
